mark_split.label: Simplify to a standard log integral

verification.note: Source: Baby Bullet-Q, Senior Inter Maths-2B (Sri Publishers, Machilipatnam), book p.70 — SAQ chapter 10 'Definite Integrals', answer 86, the first item on the page (a new sub-topic — this is no longer a King's-property question). insider_note: tan(x/2) = t is the universal substitution for any rational function of sinx and cosx — when no King's-property shortcut is visible, this is always the fallback.

steps.label: Substitute tan(x/2) = t
steps.margin_note: First two marks. Both the cosx formula and the dx formula must be written in terms of t.
steps.memory_tip: tan(x/2) = t gives cosx = (1−t²)/(1+t²) and dx = 2dt/(1+t²) — a fixed pair to memorise together.
lines: Also x = 0 ⇒ t = 0; x = π/2 ⇒ t = tan(π/4) = 1
steps.why: The half-angle substitution tan(x/2) = t turns any rational combination of sinx and cosx into a rational function of t, which can then be integrated by partial fractions or a standard formula.
common_mistakes: Mixing up the formulas for sinx and cosx in terms of t.
Forgetting to convert the limits from x-values to the corresponding t-values.

steps.label: Simplify to a standard log integral
steps.margin_note: One mark. Clearing the compound fraction leaves a plain a² − t² denominator.
steps.memory_tip: 4(1+t²) + 5(1−t²) always simplifies to 9 − t² for this exact denominator — check the arithmetic collapses this way.
steps.why: Multiplying every term by (1+t²) clears the compound fraction, and 4(1+t²) + 5(1−t²) collapses to 9 − t², a standard a² − x² form with a = 3.
common_mistakes: Losing the factor of 2 from dx = 2dt/(1+t²) when clearing the fraction.
Simplifying 4(1+t²)+5(1−t²) incorrectly, e.g. getting 9+t² instead of 9−t².

steps.label: Evaluate the limits
steps.margin_note: The last mark. log(4/2) simplifies to log2 directly.
steps.why: The standard formula for ∫dx/(a²−x²) with a = 3 gives a log ratio; evaluating it at t = 1 and t = 0 leaves log2 minus log1, and log1 = 0 removes the second term entirely.
common_mistakes: Forgetting the outer factor of 1/(2·3) = 1/6, which combines with the leading 2 to give 1/3.
Leaving log1 in the answer instead of recognising it equals 0.
